title: The order blesses the Residency's first coin
summary: At Tolley's asking, Beathag Ruadh and the priests of Òrd Mhacha bless the new-struck coin in the temple at Cathair dhearg, naming both horses of the rite, Dubh Sainglenn and Liath Macha. Fearghas mac Mhuirich stands his place and says the words, though he watches the Residency clerk carry the satchel out and finds he cannot say why the morning troubles him.

title: Three priests will not stand for the blessing
summary: Three of the younger priests of Òrd Mhacha stand apart at the back of the temple hall rather than take their places for the blessing of the coin. Beathag Ruadh lets it pass unremarked before the Residency's clerk, and tells Fearghas mac Mhuirich only that the order answers for the rite done rightly, not for the road a rightly blessed thing afterward walks.

title: A penny at the door of the warm springs
summary: The bath-house the Administration built at the warm springs near Muileann ruadh opens to Dia-thìrich two days of the week, at a penny the door, for water the district had bathed in unasked since before any custodian's roll began. Catrìona nic Eachainn pays her penny and finds the water unchanged and only the door made new.

title: Artair mac Iain seated after ten empty years
summary: The Council of Custodians, unable to agree a head since Alasdair Liath's death, seats Artair mac Iain of the eastern shires as high custodian, six-and-fifty years old, in the hall where Tormod mac Ailein once signed the treaty. Fearghas mac Mhuirich says the order's blessing over him, both horses named.

title: The guild raises a daughter town
summary: As Muileann chiar's lanes fill past holding, the silver guild raises a second town a mile to the west for its carters and coal-breakers, under the old town's own name. The custodians' rolls thereafter call them the old town and the new, and do not always trouble to say which they mean.

title: Silversmiths settle at Muileann bhàn
summary: Silversmiths take up the carters' road at Muileann bhàn a day south of the silver town and work the guild's bar into brooches and clasps for the humans' own market, where a worked piece sells for far more than a bar of it ever did. It becomes the one craft of the island sold over the sea under its own maker's mark.

title: The guild refuses the Company's price a third time
summary: The Company asks a third time that the silver guild sell at the Company's own price, naming a magistrate at Ros dhomhain who might rule the question. The seven refiners of the guild hall vote it down without one dissenting hand. Catrìona nic Eachainn, in the hall for the vote, counts it the one table on the island where the Dia-thìrich still set a price.

title: The second cheapening cried at the market crosses
summary: A Residency crier reads the second cheapening of the barter table at every market cross without a custodian's council having seen it beforehand. Word of it reaches Muileann chiar three days after Cathair dhearg, carried by a carter who had heard it cried at Baile Mòr fhionn.

title: The wool of Baile Mòr fhionn left to the moths
summary: Finding a fleece worth under the new table what half a fleece was worth before, the weavers of Baile Mòr fhionn stop bringing wool to the humans' market and load it for their own crossing instead. The Company, holding the only deep-water berths on that coast, refuses them the freight, and the wool sits two winters in the warehouses.

title: Caol fhiadhaich sells eleven of its boats
summary: Called for the first time in marks rather than in kind, the harbour dues at Caol fhiadhaich cannot be raised any way but by selling boats. Eleven of two-and-twenty go to the Company at its own asking price, and the men who sailed them go into the pits the following season under Company contracts.

title: The washing-women name the king's daughter
summary: At the stream below the camp of Àth ìseal, the eldest of the washing-women first says aloud what the wash-stones had for some seasons only thought: that a girl of the camp who does not age as other children age may be of the old line of kings, and names her nighean an rìgh. Most of the camp says they do not believe it and use the name anyway.

title: Fearghas refuses to bless the second coin
summary: Asked to bless the Administration's larger second coin as the first was blessed, Fearghas mac Mhuirich, now eldest of the order at Cathair dhearg since Beathag Ruadh's death, tells the order he will not say the words, holding that a rite for a wheel cannot answer a road that turns only one way. None of the order says the words in his place.

title: The Residency notes the order divided
summary: Word of Fearghas mac Mhuirich's refusal reaches the Residency within the month. Tolley, near his own retiring, does not send for him; the Residency's letter-book records only that the order of Òrd Mhacha at the capital is divided on a religious nicety, and does not say what the nicety was.

title: Dòmhnall Maor dies at Muileann chrom
summary: Dòmhnall mac Raghnaill Maor, overseer of the coal country five-and-twenty years and signer of the granary order that stood against Catrìona nic Eachainn's strike, dies at Muileann chrom in his sixty-seventh year. Word reaches Muileann chiar by carter, and the guild hall names him a hard man gone before a harder trade going on.

title: Iain Maor takes the overseer's staff
summary: The staff passes to Dòmhnall Maor's son Iain, seven-and-thirty, first of the overseer's line schooled at the Mission at Ros dhomhain, who is said to keep his household in Dia-thìris and his reports to the Company in the humans' tongue and to walk the galleries himself.

title: Fearghas leaves the capital's temple for Cnoc bheag
summary: Fearghas mac Mhuirich walks north with eleven of the order who think as he does, to the sacred forest at Cnoc bheag. Griogair, eldest of those who stay at Cathair dhearg, walks with them as far as the north road and calls it two roads to the one rite rather than a falling-out.

title: The dissenters' first fire under the oaks
summary: Custodians without seats and priests without a temple begin to gather at the forest of Cnoc bheag through the summer, until the grove holds near as many of one kind as the other. On the last evening of the spring Fearghas mac Mhuirich lights the first fire there and says the rite of the two horses whole.
